notes: Abu Ghraib libel offer-of-amends assessment; Eady J's findings on gravity, security risk and belated apology are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Campbell-James v Guardian: Abu Ghraib libel compensation under offer of amends
key_facts: The Guardian published an article linking Col Jonathan Campbell-James to the Abu Ghraib torture scandal though he was not in Iraq when the abuses occurred.
The headline and pull-quote suggested UK ministers had given a false impression about British involvement in prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib.
The claimant, an Arabic-speaking Intelligence Corps officer, gave evidence of serious security risk and lasting career damage in the Middle East.
The Guardian delayed an offer of amends for about three months and initially relied on qualified privilege and fair comment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 3(5) assessment of compensation after acceptance of an unqualified offer of amends in libel proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Starting point damages of £90,000 were reduced by 35% to £58,500 to reflect the belated offer of amends and published apology.
enrichment.ratio: Serious libels touching loyalty and professional honour warrant a high starting award, but defendants using the offer-of-amends regime are entitled to a significant discount; delay, dismissive conduct and security risks may reduce that discount.
legal_issues: Appropriate starting point for a grave libel linking a serving officer to torture
Extent of discount for belated offer of amends and apology
Relevance of security risk and Middle Eastern republication
Whether qualified privilege or fair comment justified initial publication
linked_authorities: John v MGN Ltd [1997] QB 586
Nail v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2005] 1 All ER 1040
Abu v MGN Ltd [2003] 1 WLR 2201

confidence.notes: Award, reasoning on starting point and discount, and factual background are all clearly recorded.

notes: Attempted murder sentencing after CJA 2003; section 244 transitional error and proportionality with murder tariffs are central.

enrichment.short_title: R v Ford: attempted murder sentence after Criminal Justice Act 2003 reforms
key_facts: Kevin Ford was convicted after trial of two counts of attempted murder following a gangland-style shooting in Sheffield in June 2004.
He fired three shots at two men in a car, seriously injuring one victim who required liver surgery.
The trial judge sentenced him to 30 years on each count, assuming section 244 release at half the term applied.
The offence predated 4 April 2005 so the pre-section 244 two-thirds release regime applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence referred to the Full Court with leave granted.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the 30-year sentence was quashed and replaced with 24 years concurrent on each count.
enrichment.ratio: Courts may upwardly adjust sentences for the most serious attempted murders to maintain proportionality with the schedule 21 murder starting point, but the judge erred in applying section 244 to an offence committed before its commencement; release probabilities under the correct regime must be reflected.
legal_issues: Whether section 244 applied to an offence committed on 26 June 2004
Whether upward adjustment of attempted murder sentences to mirror new murder tariffs is lawful
Article 7 ECHR objection to judicial increases pending dangerous-offender provisions
What discount should reflect the difference between murder and attempted murder
linked_authorities: R v Sullivan, Gibbs, Elenor and Elenor [2005] 1 Cr App R(S) 308
Attorney-General's Reference No 36 of 1996 (R v Johnson) [1997] 1 Cr App R(S) 633

confidence.notes: Statutory commencement point, substituted sentence and sentencing principles are explicitly reasoned.

notes: Case stated on prosecution adjournment after CPS witness warning failure; convictions quashed for lack of reasons.

enrichment.short_title: Essen v DPP: prosecution adjournment and quashed drink-driving convictions
key_facts: Miss Essen was convicted of driving while unfit through drink or drugs and careless driving after a protracted magistrates' trial.
On 30 December 2002 the defence and witnesses attended but no prosecution witnesses attended because the CPS had failed to warn them.
The justices granted a prosecution adjournment over defence opposition; no reasons for that decision were recorded.
The trial resumed nearly a year later after extensive legal argument on toxicology and continuity evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Colchester Magistrates' Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the adjournment decision was set aside and both convictions were quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates grant a prosecution adjournment after the CPS alone is at fault for witness non-attendance and give no reasons, the court cannot uphold the decision; equality-of-arms does not require identical treatment of convenience-based defence adjournments and prosecution failures.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of a defence adjournment precluded granting a prosecution adjournment on the same day
Wednesbury review of magistrates' adjournment discretion
Timeliness of challenging an interlocutory adjournment by case stated after conviction
Whether a stay was required because of part-heard delay
linked_authorities: R (Walden and Stern) v Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court [2002] EWHC 708 (Admin)
R v Hereford Magistrates' Court ex parte Rowlands [1998] QB 110
R v Rochford Justices ex parte Buck (1979) 68 Cr App R 114

confidence.notes: Outcome and adjournment reasoning are clear though Sedley LJ also raised wider jurisdictional concerns.

notes: Litigant-in-person family appeals; Ward LJ dismissed five applications including expired and academic orders.

enrichment.short_title: O v O: dismissal of multiple family injunction and residence appeals
key_facts: Mr Oritsejaro applied for permission to appeal five separate county court orders arising from matrimonial proceedings.
HHJ Hornby ordered him to leave the matrimonial home and granted non-molestation injunctions after finding domestic violence.
HHJ Roberts made a residence order in the mother's favour when the father failed to attend; a prohibited steps order application failed because the children were already in Nigeria.
Several challenged orders had expired or were academic by the time of the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Five renewed applications for permission to appeal listed before Ward LJ.
enrichment.outcome: All applications dismissed; the court held there was no jurisdiction to appeal a refusal of permission to appeal and declined academic appeals.
enrichment.ratio: Findings of domestic violence supported by medical and police evidence will not be overturned where the judge disbelieved the applicant; expired or academic orders cannot be appealed, and section 54(4) bars appeal against refusal of permission to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether injunction and ouster orders were properly made under domestic violence legislation
Jurisdiction to appeal a refusal of permission to appeal
Whether a residence order made in absence should be set aside under CPR 39.3
Whether appeals against expired or academic orders should be entertained

confidence.notes: Disposal of each application is stated clearly though many subsidiary written points were not resolved individually.

notes: DLA supersession and renewal appeal for child with asthma/eczema; Commissioner error on post-2001 award accepted.

enrichment.short_title: Abbas v DWP: disability living allowance supersession and renewal

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Sukaina Abbas, a child with asthma, eczema and hay fever, had received DLA care component at the highest rate since 1992.
In September 2000 the Secretary of State superseded the 1997 award for change in circumstances and refused renewal from January 2001.
The Commissioner found the tribunal erred by failing to address the supersession criterion and awarded the lowest care rate for the residue of the 1997 period.
The Commissioner wrongly declined to decide entitlement after 24 January 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned application for permission to appeal from a Social Security Commissioner decision, with appeal to follow.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the refusal to award benefit after 24 January 2001 was set aside on the basis of a Secretary of State undertaking to pay the lowest care rate until 31 December 2005.
enrichment.ratio: Supersession under section 10 requires a relevant change of circumstances since the prior award; where a Commissioner finds legal error he may substitute a lowest-rate award if section 72(1)(a) is satisfied, and must also determine renewal entitlement for the subsequent claim period.
legal_issues: Construction of section 72 care component day, night and significant-portion conditions
Whether the tribunal addressed the supersession change-of-circumstances test
Commissioner's power under section 14(8) to substitute findings and decisions
Whether adjournment should be granted where the litigation friend could not attend

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, Commissioner findings and final undertaking-based remedy are comprehensively explained.

notes: Commercial lease reinstatement preliminary issues; Buxton LJ upheld conjunctive construction of clause 2(8)(B).

enrichment.short_title: Fairgate v Citibank: lease reinstatement clauses 2(8)(A) and (B)
key_facts: Citibank held a lease of Kensington High Street offices with covenants to yield up repaired and, if required, to remove fixtures or reinstate to Third and Fourth Schedule specifications.
Fairgate served notice invoking both clause 2(8)(B)(i) removal and 2(8)(B)(ii) specification works before expiry in 2002.
Citibank argued the sub-clauses were mutually exclusive alternatives and the notice was invalid for uncertainty.
Proceedings claimed damages for breach of yield-up and reinstatement covenants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against preliminary issue declarations on lease construction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; clauses 2(8)(B)(i) and (ii) are not alternatives and the August 2002 notice was valid.
enrichment.ratio: Absent a conjunction, sub-clauses 2(8)(B)(i) and (ii) may be invoked together; where both apply, specification works under (ii) prevail over inconsistent removal or repair obligations under (i) or 2(8)(A), and a general notice is not void merely because detailed scope awaits surveyor agreement.
legal_issues: Whether clause 2(8)(B)(i) and (ii) are mutually exclusive alternatives
Validity of a notice invoking both reinstatement sub-clauses
Relationship between clauses 2(8)(A) and (B)
Effect of section 18(1) cap if only clause 2(8)(A) applied
linked_authorities: Proudfoot v Hart (1890) 25 QBD 42

confidence.notes: Three preliminary declarations and construction reasoning are explicit and complete.

notes: Rape conviction appeal; section 41 cross-examination ruling and kerb-crawling evidence upheld, sentence reduced.

enrichment.short_title: R v Abdelrahman: rape conviction appeal and section 41 ruling

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: The appellant was convicted of raping an 18-year-old prostitute who identified his car, employment at Medway Hospital and aspects of his Gillingham flat.
The prosecution adduced evidence of the appellant speaking to prostitutes near Rochester station after he denied interest in prostitutes.
The judge refused cross-examination about alleged previous false rape complaints for lack of evidential basis that they were untrue.
The jury acquitted him of a related firearm offence but convicted on rape.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge; sentence appeal followed.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed as safe; sentence appeal allowed and six years was reduced to five years.
enrichment.ratio: Evidence of consorting with prostitutes is admissible to rebut a denial of interest in prostitution; section 41 excludes cross-examination about previous sexual behaviour where the purpose is to impugn credibility without a proper evidential basis that prior complaints were false.
legal_issues: Admissibility and section 78 exclusion of kerb-crawling evidence
Whether cross-examination about previous rape allegations was permitted under section 41
Safety of conviction where judge invited speculation then corrected the summing-up
Appropriate sentence under Millberry guidelines
linked_authorities: RT and MH [2001] EWCA Crim 1877
Funderburk (1990) 90 Cr App R 466
C and B [2003] EWCA Crim 29

notes: Pensions indemnity amendment refused by Lightman J; Mance LJ granted expedited renewed permission to appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Mandrake v Countrywide: amendment to pensions indemnity loss-of-opportunity claim
key_facts: Mandrake claimed Countrywide was liable under an indemnity deed for Phase 2 pensions review compensation payments.
In December 2004, after 18 months of litigation, the claimants sought to amend to add loss-of-opportunity damages for failure to pay the indemnity.
Lightman J refused amendment because Sprung v Royal Insurance bound him to hold such a claim bad in law and because the July 2005 trial date would be lost.
The proposed amendment alleged the indemnity was critical to turning around the company.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal from refusal to allow amendment to points of claim.
enrichment.outcome: Mance LJ adjourned for expedited inter partes hearing with substantive appeal to follow if permission granted.
enrichment.ratio: Refusal of a late amendment may be reviewable where the judge may have mischaracterised the claimant's proposal for preliminary determination of the Sprung point and overstated prejudice from loss of a trial date; Sprung remains binding but may warrant House of Lords reconsideration.
legal_issues: Whether damages are recoverable for failure to pay an indemnity under Sprung v Royal Insurance
Case management discretion to refuse late amendment
Whether limiting trial to foreseeability without causation was appropriate
Prejudice from losing a fixed trial date
linked_authorities: Sprung v Royal Insurance [1999] 1 Lloyd's Rep IR 111
Baird Textiles Holdings Ltd v Marks and Spencer Plc [2001] EWCA Civ 274

confidence.notes: Interlocutory permission decision is clear though final merits of the Sprung point remain unresolved.

notes: Swingers libel s.3(5) assessment with reference innuendo and Burstein background context; £9,000 award.

enrichment.short_title: Turner v News of the World: swinging libel and Burstein background context
key_facts: The News of the World published a swinging article identifying Mr Turner only through a photograph of his former wife Arisara Turner.
The sting was that he pressurised her to have sex with other men at a Coventry club though an offer of amends accepted that allegation was false.
The defendant relied on Burstein background context including fetish club attendance, explicit modelling and earlier tabloid publicity initiated by the claimant.
The claimant complained of initial delay and a startling Burstein mitigation plea later withdrawn in part.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 3(5) assessment of compensation after unqualified offer of amends in a reference-innuendo libel claim.
enrichment.outcome: Starting point £15,000 reduced by 40% to £9,000 compensation from News Group Newspapers Ltd.
enrichment.ratio: Directly relevant background context under Burstein may be admissible on quantification even after an offer of amends if notified beforehand; reference-innuendo and prior tabloid exposure reduce gravity and hurt feelings, and initial dismissive conduct may reduce the offer-of-amends discount.
legal_issues: Application of Burstein to section 3(5) assessments
Admissibility of fetish club, modelling and prior press publicity as background context
Appropriate starting point and discount for unqualified offer of amends
Whether defendant conduct aggravated injury after accepting the offer
linked_authorities: Burstein v Times Newspapers Ltd [2001] 1 WLR 57
Abu v MGN Ltd [2003] 1 WLR 2201
Nail v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2005] 1 All ER 1040

notes: Road-rage section 18 sentence appeal dismissed; court clarified non-guideline AG reference cases.

enrichment.short_title: R v Lyon: road rage section 18 sentence and sentencing authorities
key_facts: After a traffic dispute the appellant head-butted Mr Opanuga, knocked him unconscious and was heard to use a racial insult.
The victim suffered severe facial injuries requiring a metal plate and lasting nerve damage, pain and psychological harm.
The appellant was convicted of causing grievous bodily harm with intent and dangerous driving.
He was sentenced to five years on count 1 and one month concurrent on count 2, with a two-year driving disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence with leave granted by the Full Court after refusal by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; five years was held a fully justified sentence for the section 18 offence.
enrichment.ratio: Road rage is an aggravating context for section 18 offences but is not a separate sentencing category; isolated Attorney-General reference and leave decisions do not set general tariffs, and unduly lenient reference judgments focus on the minimum proper sentence rather than sentencing brackets.
legal_issues: Whether five years was manifestly excessive for a road-rage section 18 offence
Status of Attorney-General's Reference No 88 of 2000 and R v Holmes as sentencing guides
Relevance of good character and loss of business
Whether racial aggravation affected the sentence
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's Reference No 88 of 2000 [2001] EWCA Crim 68
R v Holmes [1997] EWCA Crim 1288
Attorney-General's Reference No 36 of 1996 (R v Johnson) [1997] 1 Cr App R(S) 633
